title: Queen against a pawn on the seventh
summary: With checks and pins, the queen puts the black king in front of its own pawn, and each time our king takes a step.
step.intro: A pawn on the seventh, one square from becoming a queen, and our king far away on a8. It looks like a lost race, but it isn't. Against a centre pawn or a knight's pawn, the queen alone wins the time our king needs. Right now she watches e1, but she cannot take the pawn: the black king defends it. So the question of this lesson is: how do we bring our king over without letting the pawn promote?
step.idea: This is the position we are aiming for. The black king stands on e1, in front of its own pawn. As long as it stays there, the pawn cannot move. Black will need a whole move just to step the king aside, and that move is our gift: the white king takes one step towards the pawn. Then the queen forces the king back to e1, and it all happens again.
step.stairs: Let's drive the black king to e1. The queen comes in with checks, each one closer to the pawn, never touching the king. Start from the centre.
step.stairs.hint: A check from a central square the black king can't reach. Then another check, a little closer.
step.stairs.done: A staircase of checks: d4, e3 and d3. In the end the black king had no choice. On c1 it would abandon the pawn and the queen would take on e2. So it went to e1, in front of it. Starting with Qf2, pinning the pawn, also worked.
step.tempo: The black king is in front of the pawn. This move is free: bring your king closer. Then, when Black steps the king aside, hold the pawn.
step.tempo.hint: First a king step towards the pawn. Then, with the black king beside the pawn, find a square where the queen attacks the pawn and ties it to the king.
step.tempo.done: Kb7 and, with the black king on f2, Qd2: the pawn is pinned. If it moves, its own king is in check. Qc2 pins the same way, and the checks Qd4+ and Qf5+ also kept control.
step.again: The black king ran to f1. Now repeat the staircase on this side: checks until it goes back to e1.
step.again.hint: A check from a distance, from a square the black king can't reach. The target is the same as before: the king in front of the pawn.
step.again.done: Qf4+, Qe3+ and Qf3+. The black king is back on e1 and ours is already on b7. That is one full cycle, and it earned us a free king move.
step.cycle: From here on, you repeat. Every cycle the black king goes in front of the pawn and our king gains a square: c6, d5, e4, d3. Once it is close, the queen takes the pawn and you are in the king and queen mate you already know. No hurry: as long as you run the cycle properly, the pawn stays where it is.
step.quiet: Sometimes the black king moves further away, like here on c2, two files from the pawn. No check helps. Find the quiet move that attacks the pawn up close.
step.quiet.hint: The queen right next to the pawn, on a square the black king can't take, which also takes d2 and d3 away from it.
step.quiet.done: Qe3. The black king had to go back to d1 to defend the pawn, and Qd3+ put it on e1 again. A quiet move is technique too.
step.arrive: Our king has arrived. Time to finish: how do you make sure the queen can take the pawn?
step.arrive.hint: The queen can take on e2 safely if our king defends that square.
step.arrive.done: Kd3, and after Kc1, Qxe2. With the pawn gone, it is the king and queen mate. Kc3 on the second move also won and set up the mate directly.
step.block: A word of caution about our king. Here it stands on d5 and looks well placed, but it is in the way: it closes the d-file for the queen. Without checks along the d-file there is no way to put the black king on e1, and the pawn promotes or costs us the queen. It's a draw. When you bring the king closer, don't stop in front of the queen's lines.
step.others: Why does this lesson only talk about centre and knight's pawns? With a bishop's pawn or a rook's pawn, the defender has a trick: the king goes to the corner. Look here: if the queen takes on c2, Black has no move, and it's stalemate. Those draws, and when you can win anyway, are for the next lesson.
step.recap: What to take with you. One: checks and pins, never touching the king, until the black king stands in front of its own pawn. Two: every time that happens, our king takes a step. Three: repeat until the king is close, without letting it block the queen's lines. This works against centre and knight's pawns.
step.finish: Now the starting position, against the machine, and it defends well: sometimes it runs away from the pawn instead of stepping in front of it. If the pawn is left alone, attack it. If not, run the cycle. Finish with mate.
ex.e01: White to play. The black king is in front of the pawn. How do you use this move?
ex.e01.hint: Right now the pawn can't move. Which of your pieces is far from the action?
ex.e01.solution: Kg7 (or Kh7). The king uses the free move to walk towards the pawn. Moving the queen here only wastes the time the technique has earned.
ex.e02: White to play. The black king has stepped away from the front of the pawn. How do you hold the pawn?
ex.e02.hint: No check needed. The pawn and the black king are on the same rank.
ex.e02.solution: Qe2: the pawn is pinned, because moving it would put its king in check. Qf2 pins the same way, and the checks Qe4+ and Qc5+ also keep control.
ex.e03: White to play. Put the black king in front of the pawn.
ex.e03.hint: A check that leaves the black king only one good square.
ex.e03.solution: Qe3+. The king has to go to d1, in front of the pawn. If it goes to f1, it abandons the pawn and the queen takes on d2.
ex.e04: White to play. The black king is two files away from the pawn. Get it in front of the pawn and use the move you gain.
ex.e04.hint: Start with a quiet queen move, right next to the pawn. Then a check, and then the free move.
ex.e04.solution: Qd3, attacking the pawn; the best defence is the king going to e1. Qe3+ pushes it to d1, in front of the pawn, and our king walks: Ke5 (Kf5 and Kg5 also work).
ex.e05: White to play. The queen is attacked by the pawn. Where does she go?
ex.e05.hint: Running away is not enough: the queen has to keep holding the pawn.
ex.e05.solution: Qh2: the pawn is pinned along the rank, and the best defence is the king going to f1. Then Qf4+, and the king must choose between g1, in front of the pawn, and leaving it. Knight's pawn, same technique. Qh4+ on the first move also won.
ex.e06: White to play. Our king is close. Win the pawn.
ex.e06.hint: The queen already attacks the pawn, but it is defended. Who can help?
ex.e06.solution: Ke3: now our king also defends d2. After Kf1, Qxd2, and it's the king and queen mate. Kf3 on the second move also won.
ex.e07: White to play. Our king is close, but the queen needs a good check. Which one?
ex.e07.hint: The checks on the c-file land right next to the black king. Look for another line.
ex.e07.solution: Qd8+ (or Qd7+). Along the d-file the queen checks from a distance and drives the black king off d2 without it being able to take her. With our king on d5 that file would be closed, and it would be a draw.
ex.e08: White to play. The pawn is on d2 with the black king on c1, and the queen is far away. Find the move that holds everything.
ex.e08.hint: There is a quiet move: a diagonal that runs through the pawn and ends at the king.
ex.e08.solution: Qh6: along the h6-c1 diagonal the pawn is pinned. The king steps to c2, and Qh2 pins it again, now along the rank. Qc7+ on the first move also won, and on the second the checks Qc6+ and Qg6+ work too.
ex.e09: White to play. The queen is in the corner, far from the pawn. Walk down the staircase of checks.
ex.e09.hint: Checks that come closer every move, never touching the king. Start where the black king can't reach.
ex.e09.solution: Qa4+ (or Qa2+), Kc1, Qc4+ (or Qf4, pinning the pawn), Kb1 and Qd3+ (or Qb3+). The black king goes back to c1, and one more check, Qc3+, puts it on d1, in front of the pawn.
ex.e10: White to play. A knight's pawn on b2. Get the black king in front of the pawn.
ex.e10.hint: The same staircase as with the centre pawn: checks that come closer until the black king has to choose between b1 and giving up the pawn.
ex.e10.solution: Qc4+ (or Qe2+), Kd1, Qb3+ (or Qd3+), Kc1 and Qc3+. Now the black king goes to b1, in front of the pawn, or to d1, and the pawn falls.
key.start: The starting position of the lesson, our own: pawn on e2, black king beside it, our king on a8. The tablebase says it wins.
key.front: The black king on e1, in front of the pawn: the moment our king gains a move.
key.dang: The starting position of Danghiangmanh's "Queen vs Pawn" study on Lichess: the same technique with the queen coming from h8.
key.block: White king on d5, queen on c8: the king closes the queen's d-file and it's a draw. Diagram from Wikipedia.
history: The technique is old and appears in every manual: Wikipedia cites it from Reuben Fine's Basic Chess Endings, from 1941, and Jesús de la Villa opens the queen against pawn chapter of his 100 Endgames You Must Know with it. What always interested the analysts were the exceptions. Giambattista Lolli published a study with a bishop's pawn in 1763, and the ending turned up in games between strong players: Alatortsev beat Chekhover in 1937 against a bishop's pawn on the sixth, and Van Wely and Leko drew in 1996 precisely because of the bishop's pawn. With a centre or knight's pawn there is no trick: the queen wins.
practice: Now against the clock, or without it. The pawn is on the seventh and your king is far away. Staircase of checks, king in front of the pawn, one step at a time.
